steps.label: Footprint and entities
steps.intro: Where the group operates, whose personal data it holds, and the regulated roles that decide which laws apply. These answers set scope; they are never scored.

steps.label: Data and platforms
steps.intro: The kinds of data you hold, where each sits today, and the platforms that hold it.

steps.label: Sovereignty requirement
steps.intro: How much control the board wants over its data, on top of what the law requires. The required level of each kind of data is the higher of the two.

steps.label: Location, transfers and keys
steps.intro: How data location is enforced, what covers transfers, and who holds the keys.

steps.label: Operations and third parties
steps.intro: Who can reach your data, what your contracts give you, and how ready you are to leave a provider.

steps.label: AI and governance
steps.intro: AI data location and governance, ownership, incident reporting and assurance.

steps.label: Outcome preferences
steps.intro: How the board wants remediation sequenced. Not scored.

questions.text: Where is your group headquartered?
basis: Default allowed zone (DESIGN 2.6); US person test, 28 CFR Part 202

questions.text: For each region: do you have a legal entity, branch or office there, and do you hold personal data about people located there (customers, employees, users)?
questions.help: The EU and EEA count as one region. Japan, Hong Kong, Australia and New Zealand are separate rows.

columns.label: We have an entity or office here
We hold personal data of people here

basis: GDPR Art. 3(1)-(2); UK GDPR Art. 3; AI Act Art. 2(1); PDPA; DPDP s.3; PIPL Art. 3

questions.text: Which sector best describes your main business?
questions.help: A SaaS or cloud provider choosing digital infrastructure is treated as a cloud computing service provider under NIS2.

options.label: Financial market infrastructure (trading venues, central counterparties)
Payments, e-money, investment, crypto-assets and other financial services
Healthcare providers, pharmaceutical and medical-device manufacturing
Digital infrastructure (cloud, data centres, CDN, DNS, trust services, telecoms)
Managed IT or managed security services for other businesses
Manufacturing of medical devices, electronics, electrical equipment, machinery or vehicles
Online marketplaces, search engines or social networks
Professional, consulting or IT services that are not managed IT services

basis: NIS2 Annexes I and II; NIS2 Art. 6(30) and recital 33 (SaaS as a cloud computing service)

questions.text: Roughly how large is the group? (headcount and annual turnover, euro equivalent, including companies you control)
basis: NIS2 Art. 2(1) and Recommendation 2003/361/EC; CCPA revenue test; Privacy Act small-business threshold

questions.text: For the exposure view: what was last year's worldwide turnover, and the balance-sheet total?
basis: GDPR Art. 83(4)-(5); NIS2 Art. 34; AI Act Art. 99; Recommendation 2003/361/EC Art. 2

questions.text: In which EU and EEA countries do you have entities or offices?
basis: NIS2 national transposition; national schemes (SecNumCloud, C5)

questions.text: In which US states do you have customers or employees whose personal data you hold?

options.label: Other states with comprehensive privacy laws

basis: CCPA (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140); other state comprehensive privacy laws

questions.text: Which of these describe your organisation or a group company? Select all that apply.

options.label: EU investment firm, asset manager or trading venue
EU insurer, reinsurer or occupational pension fund
Other EU financial entity under DORA
We provide ICT services to EU financial entities
We are designated a critical ICT third-party provider under DORA
PRA-regulated (bank, building society, PRA-designated investment firm, insurer)
Designated as a UK critical third party
RBI-authorised payment system operator, or part of its payment ecosystem
HIPAA covered entity or business associate
Cloud supplier to US federal agencies
Operator of critical infrastructure in any country
We provide cloud or data-processing services to customers
We sell software or connected products in the EU

basis: DORA Art. 2; PRA SS1/21 and FCA PS21/3; FSMA 2000 ss.312L-312Z (critical third parties); MAS, APRA, HKMA, RBI; 23 NYCRR 500; SEC Form 8-K; 45 CFR 160.103; Data Act Ch. VI; CRA

questions.text: Under NIS2: how have you classified yourselves, and are you one of the special entity types?

options.label: Public electronic communications network or service

questions.text: Are you responsible for critical infrastructure under any of these regimes?

options.label: UK relevant digital service provider (cloud, marketplace, search)

basis: SOCI Act 2018; UK NIS Regulations 2018; Singapore Cybersecurity Act 2018; PIPL Art. 40

questions.text: How does your organisation use AI today? Select all that apply.

options.label: We do not use AI in production
We use AI tools or third-party models for internal work
We use AI in decisions about people (credit, insurance pricing, hiring, biometric identification, access to essential services)
We build AI systems and sell or deploy them for others
We train or provide general-purpose AI models
We put third-party AI models into products sold under our name

basis: AI Act Art. 2(1), 3, 25(1), Annex III items 1, 4, 5(b), 5(c)

questions.text: Which kinds of data do you hold? Select all that apply.

options.label: Personal data about customers, employees or users
Sensitive personal data: health, genetic, biometric, ethnicity, beliefs, sex life or orientation, criminal records
Financial account, card and payment-transaction data
Datasets used to train or fine-tune AI models
Trade secrets, source code and other commercially sensitive non-personal data
Classified data, or data held for a government client under contract restrictions

basis: GDPR Art. 4(1), 9, 10; RBI payment data; Data Act Art. 32 (non-personal data)

questions.text: Roughly how many people's personal records do you hold in total?
basis: 28 CFR 202.205 thresholds; CCPA 100,000 test; CAC 2024 Provisions

questions.text: For each kind of data you hold: where is it stored and processed today, and where are its backups and disaster-recovery copies?
questions.help: The EU and EEA count as one region.
basis: GDPR Ch. V (EEA as one area); RBI Storage of Payment System Data; PIPL Art. 40; NIST SP 800-53 SA-9(5)

questions.text: Is there a current map of where your data flows, with records of processing, updated in the last 12 months?
basis: GDPR Art. 30; EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 step 1

questions.text: Which platforms run your production systems and hold your data? Select all that apply.
questions.help: Provider names are examples only; S7 sources each one.

options.label: Hyperscaler technology run by an independent local operator
A locally owned cloud in APAC

basis: Platform playbook scope (S7); provider parent jurisdiction is a fact, never a score (D3)

questions.text: Where are the parent companies of the providers that hold your regulated data headquartered?
questions.help: Refines the default derived from your platforms.
basis: CLOUD Act, 18 U.S.C. § 2713 (possession, custody or control)

questions.text: For each kind of data on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud: which kinds of service hold it?
questions.help: Used only to focus the cloud advisory on the services you use. Never scored.

options.label: Collaboration SaaS (for example Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace)

basis: Sovereign Cloud Advisory scope (PLAN S7, D17); service families, not products (D19)

questions.text: Beyond what the law requires, how much control does the board want over its data?
questions.help: Sets the client's choice for every kind of data selected; the workshop refines it per kind of data.

options.label: Keep the data in our chosen region
Keep it in region and hold the keys, so the provider cannot read it without us
Have it run and supported only by staff in our region through a local entity
Make it immune from foreign laws, or keep it disconnected

basis: EU Cloud Sovereignty Framework SEAL levels (LTM mapping, not the Commission's)

questions.text: For each kind of data: which level do you need, in which region(s) may it sit, and which platforms hold it?
basis: As L1; tender minimum SEALs translated with the LTM mapping

questions.text: How is the rule on where data may be stored enforced?

options.label: Technically enforced everywhere: policies block deployments outside the allowed regions
Enforced on some platforms or accounts only
By convention or manual review only

basis: NIST SP 800-53 SA-9(5)

questions.text: When personal data leaves the region where it was collected (including remote access from another country), what covers it? Select all that apply.

options.label: It never leaves, including remote access
An adequacy decision or adequacy regulations
EU-US Data Privacy Framework, recipient certified
UK Extension to the DPF ("data bridge"), recipient certified
Contracts, consent or other routes required by APAC laws
Only derogations (e.g. explicit consent, contract necessity)
Some transfers have no documented basis

basis: GDPR Art. 44-46, 49; Decision (EU) 2023/1795 (appeal C-703/25 P pending); UK GDPR Art. 44A (DUAA); PDPA s.26; APP 8; APPI Art. 28; PIPA Art. 28-8; PIPL Art. 38

questions.text: For transfers under contractual clauses or BCRs: have you assessed whether the destination's laws, including government access, undermine the protection, and recorded the result?

options.label: Yes, for every such transfer, reviewed regularly, and the safeguards close the risks found
Yes, but for some transfers the destination's laws are not offset by the safeguards in place
options.help: The assessment is recorded (this control), but those transfers have no valid basis: SOV.XFER.BASIS scores 0 for them (CJEU C-311/18; EDPB Recommendations 01/2020)

options.label: For some transfers, or not reviewed

basis: CJEU C-311/18 (Schrems II); EDPB Recommendations 01/2020; ICO transfer risk assessment guidance

questions.text: US bulk sensitive data: which covered categories do you hold about US persons, and do you screen transactions that could give a country of concern access to them?
questions.help: The options are those of the screening field, which sets the control; the categories field sets a fact.

options.label: We screen and block or license covered transactions and keep records
Data linked to US government personnel or sites
We screen and block or license covered transactions and keep records

questions.text: For your most sensitive data in cloud and SaaS, who controls the encryption keys?

options.label: We hold the keys outside the provider (external key manager or our own HSM); the provider cannot use them without us
Keys in a single-tenant HSM in the provider's data centre that only we administer
We create or import keys into the provider's key service, which the provider operates
Varies: external keys on some platforms, provider keys on others
The provider creates and manages the keys
Some sensitive data is not encrypted at rest

basis: NIST SP 800-53 SC-12, SC-28; EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 Annex 2

questions.text: Have you tested that revoking your keys makes provider-held copies, including backups and caches, unreadable?

options.label: Not possible: the provider manages the key lifecycle

basis: NIST SP 800-53 SC-12

questions.text: Is regulated data encrypted at rest and in transit everywhere?

options.label: At rest everywhere; some internal traffic unencrypted

basis: GDPR Art. 32(1)(a); NIS2 Art. 21(2)(h); NIST SP 800-53 SC-8, SC-28

questions.text: Do you use confidential computing (hardware-protected enclaves) for your most sensitive data while it is being processed?
basis: LTM heuristic for L4; provider documentation sourced in S7

questions.text: When your cloud, SaaS or hosting providers need to reach your systems or data for support or operations, what happens?

options.label: Access needs our explicit, time-limited approval, and every access is logged and reviewed
Approval and logging on our main platforms, not on all SaaS
Access is logged and visible to us but needs no approval
Provider staff access under the provider's standard terms; we have no visibility

basis: NIST SP 800-53 MA-4, AC-2; GDPR Art. 28(3)(b)-(c), 32

questions.text: For services holding your most sensitive data: who operates and supports them, and under which entity and law?

options.label: Only staff located in the allowed region, employed by a locally established entity under local law, including escalations
Staff in the region, but the operating company or contract is foreign

basis: EU Cloud Sovereignty Framework SOV-4 (operational); NIST SP 800-53 PS-3

questions.text: For on-premises hardware, is remote out-of-band management (e.g. iDRAC, iLO) isolated, and is vendor call-home controlled?

options.label: Isolated management network; vendor call-home blocked or approved

basis: NIST SP 800-53 MA-4

questions.text: Do you have data-processing (or service-provider) agreements with every processor?
basis: GDPR Art. 28(3); HIPAA business associate agreements; DPDP s.8(2); CCPA § 1798.100(d); 16 CFR 314.4(f); 23 NYCRR 500.11

questions.text: For critical SaaS and cloud providers: do you know their sub-processors, and do you get advance notice and a right to object to changes?
basis: GDPR Art. 28(2), (4); DORA Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/532

questions.text: Do you know where each key SaaS and ICT provider actually stores and processes your data?
basis: NIS2 Art. 21(2)(d); EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 step 1

questions.text: Do your cloud and ICT contracts give you audit, access and inspection rights over how your data is handled?
basis: DORA Art. 30; PRA SS2/21; MAS Guidelines on Outsourcing

questions.text: Do you keep a complete register of your ICT third-party arrangements (the DORA register of information, or your regulator's equivalent)?

options.label: Complete, maintained, and submitted when requested

basis: DORA Art. 28(3); APRA CPS 230; PRA SS2/21

questions.text: Have you mapped which important business services depend on the UK designated critical third parties, and what duties stay with you?

options.label: We do not use any designated CTP

basis: UK critical third party designations from 13 Jul 2026 (FSMA 2000 ss.312L-312Z)

questions.text: If your main cloud or SaaS provider became unavailable or no longer acceptable (for example after a change in law), how ready are you to move critical services?

options.label: Documented exit plans for critical services, portable formats, and a rehearsal or partial migration done
Documented exit plans with a realistic timeline, not rehearsed
Plans for some services only, or a timeline over 18 months
No exit plan; effectively locked in

basis: DORA Art. 28(8); APRA CPS 230; PRA SS2/21; Data Act Art. 29. Exit testing is assessed in Resilience IQ

questions.text: How concentrated are your critical services on one provider?

options.label: Critical services can run on more than one provider or on-premises
One main provider, with documented alternatives for critical services
One provider hosts most critical services; the risk is assessed and accepted by the board
One provider hosts most critical services; not assessed

basis: DORA Art. 29; APRA CPS 230

questions.text: Where do your AI models run (training, fine-tuning and inference), and can the provider use your data to train its own models?

options.label: In our allowed region, and the provider contractually cannot train on our data
In our region, but the training-use terms are not confirmed
Outside our region, with contractual no-training and data-handling terms
Outside our region, terms not reviewed

basis: GDPR Ch. V for personal data in AI pipelines; AI Act Art. 10

questions.text: Have you assessed your role under the EU AI Act for each AI system, classified each system by risk, and mapped the obligations and their dates? (For UK firms: also against ICO, FCA and PRA expectations.)
basis: AI Act Art. 2, 6, 25, 26, 50, Annex III; dates per Regulation (EU) 2026/1744

questions.text: Who owns decisions on where your data and workloads may run?

options.label: One named executive, with a governance forum
Shared across teams, no single owner

basis: NIS2 Art. 20; DORA Art. 5

questions.text: Can you detect, classify and report an incident within the shortest window that applies to you (for example 1 hour under MAS notices, 4 hours under DORA, 6 hours under CERT-In directions, 12 hours under SOCI, 24 hours under NIS2, 72 hours under GDPR)?

options.label: Documented but untested, or unclear for cross-border incidents

basis: MAS TRM Notices; DORA RTS (EU) 2025/301; CERT-In Directions 2022; SOCI; NIS2 Art. 23; GDPR Art. 33

questions.text: Do the services holding your most sensitive data hold an assurance qualification that your regulators or customers recognise for that level?

options.label: Yes, a national high-assurance qualification where one applies (for example SecNumCloud, BSI C5, IRAP, MTCS, ISMAP, FedRAMP)

basis: SecNumCloud 3.2; other national schemes; EUCS not listed because not adopted

questions.text: For on-premises hardware, appliances and network equipment, have you assessed provenance against supply-chain restrictions that apply to you?
questions.help: Recorded only: not scored until its legal basis is sourced.
basis: NDAA § 889 (pending source)

questions.text: How much compliance risk will the board accept while remediating?

options.label: Moderate if residual risk is low
Flexible: cost and performance come first

basis: Roadmap sequencing only; not scored

questions.text: What is the appetite for remediation investment over the next 12 months?
basis: Roadmap sequencing; SOW sizing (consultant only); not scored

questions.text: Which outcomes matter most for the target architecture? (pick up to three)
basis: Ordering of options in the playbook (S7); not scored

controls.name: Data-location ownership
controls.means: One accountable executive owns data-location decisions, with a governance forum
controls.remedy: Name one accountable executive for where data and workloads may run, with a governance forum that records decisions and exceptions

controls.name: Data map and records of processing
controls.means: A current map of data flows and records of processing (within 12 months)
controls.remedy: Keep a data-flow map and records of processing that are reviewed at least every 12 months

controls.name: Data location
controls.means: Primary storage and processing of the class sit only in its allowed zone
controls.remedy: Move primary storage and processing of the class into its allowed region

controls.name: Region enforcement
controls.means: The location rule is enforced technically (guardrails that block non-compliant deployments)
controls.remedy: Enforce allowed regions with platform policies that block deployments elsewhere, on every platform and account

controls.name: Backup location
controls.means: Backups, replicas and disaster-recovery copies of the class sit in its allowed zone
controls.remedy: Keep backups, replicas and disaster-recovery copies of the class in its allowed region

controls.name: Transfer basis
controls.means: Every personal-data transfer (including remote access from abroad) has a valid, documented basis for each regime that restricts transfers
controls.remedy: Document a valid transfer route for every transfer, including remote access from abroad, under each law that restricts transfers

controls.name: Transfer impact assessment
controls.means: A transfer impact (EU) or transfer risk (UK) assessment is recorded for each transfer under SCCs, IDTA, Addendum or BCRs
controls.remedy: Record a transfer impact or transfer risk assessment for every transfer under contractual clauses or BCRs, and review it regularly

controls.name: US bulk data screening
controls.means: Transactions giving countries of concern access to bulk US sensitive data are screened, blocked or licensed, with records
controls.remedy: Screen data brokerage, vendor, employment and investment agreements for access by countries of concern; block or license covered transactions and keep records

controls.name: Key custody
controls.means: For sensitive data in cloud and SaaS, the client controls the keys outside the provider's control
controls.remedy: Hold the keys for sensitive data outside the provider (external key manager or your own HSM)

controls.name: Key revocation
controls.means: Key revocation that makes provider-held copies unreadable has been tested
controls.remedy: Test that revoking your keys makes provider-held copies, backups and caches unreadable

controls.name: Encryption baseline
controls.means: Regulated data is encrypted at rest and in transit everywhere
controls.remedy: Encrypt regulated data at rest and in transit everywhere, including internal traffic

controls.name: Provider access approval
controls.means: Provider support or operations access needs the client's time-limited approval and is logged and reviewed
controls.remedy: Require your explicit, time-limited approval for every provider access to systems or data, and log and review each access

controls.name: In-zone operations
controls.means: Services holding L3+ data are operated and supported only by staff in the zone, employed by a locally established entity under local law
controls.ownerRole: Head of cloud platform with Procurement
controls.remedy: Have services holding this data run and supported only by staff in the region, employed by a local entity under local law

controls.name: Out-of-band management
controls.means: On-premises out-of-band management is isolated and vendor call-home is controlled
controls.remedy: Isolate out-of-band management networks and block or approve vendor call-home

controls.name: Confidential computing
controls.means: Confidential computing protects L4 data while in use
controls.remedy: Process the most sensitive data in hardware-protected enclaves

controls.name: Processor agreements
controls.means: Processor or service-provider agreements are in place with every processor
controls.remedy: Put data-processing or service-provider agreements in place with every processor

controls.name: Sub-processor control
controls.means: Sub-processors of critical providers are known, with advance notice and a right to object to changes
controls.remedy: Know the sub-processors of critical providers, with advance notice and a right to object to changes

controls.name: Provider location visibility
controls.means: The client knows where each key provider stores and processes its data
controls.remedy: Document where each key SaaS and ICT provider stores and processes your data

controls.name: ICT third-party register
controls.means: A complete register of ICT third-party arrangements is maintained
controls.remedy: Maintain a complete register of ICT third-party arrangements, ready to submit to your regulator

controls.name: Audit rights
controls.means: Contracts give audit, access and inspection rights over data handling
controls.remedy: Secure audit, access and inspection rights over data handling in cloud and ICT contracts

controls.name: Exit plan
controls.means: Critical services have a documented, realistic exit plan (testing is owned by Resilience IQ)
controls.remedy: Document realistic exit plans for critical services, with portable formats; verify exit capability in Resilience IQ

controls.name: Provider concentration
controls.means: Concentration on one provider (including UK designated critical third parties) is assessed and managed
controls.remedy: Assess and manage concentration on one provider, including dependence on UK designated critical third parties; verify in Resilience IQ

controls.name: Assurance qualification
controls.means: Services holding L3+ data hold an assurance qualification recognised for that level
controls.remedy: Use services holding a high-assurance qualification recognised by your regulators or customers

controls.name: Jurisdictional immunity
controls.means: No provider holding the class can be compelled by a law from outside the zone, or the system is disconnected
controls.remedy: Hold this data only with providers whose parent is in the allowed region, or on disconnected systems

controls.name: AI data location
controls.means: AI training, fine-tuning and inference run in the allowed zone, and providers cannot train on client data
controls.remedy: Run AI training, fine-tuning and inference in the allowed region, with contractual no-training terms

controls.name: AI role and risk mapping
controls.means: Each AI system's role and risk class is assessed and its obligations and dates are mapped
controls.ownerRole: Head of data and AI with General Counsel
controls.remedy: Assess the AI Act role and risk class of each AI system and map its obligations and dates

controls.name: Incident reporting
controls.means: Incidents can be detected, classified and reported within the shortest window that applies
controls.remedy: Detect, classify and report incidents within the shortest regulatory window that applies, and test it in an exercise

controls.name: Hardware provenance
controls.means: Hardware and appliance provenance is assessed against supply-chain restrictions
controls.remedy: Assess hardware and appliance provenance against the supply-chain restrictions that apply to you
